title: Who turns up?
author: Simon Pollard
summary: Simon Pollard reflects on his years as a headteacher chasing empty slots on parents' evening sheets and asks what a new Department for Education study of parental engagement tells schools about the families they hear from least. He reports the authors' caution that the findings show association rather than cause, and warns against concluding that schools simply need more parents in the building. Drawing on Yates's book Fractured, he notes that the gap between what parents hope for and what they expect is socially patterned, and that many graduates have almost no close friends without a degree. He gives examples of staff whose routes through apprenticeships and further training look nothing like his own yet enrich their school. His conclusions are practical: books, libraries and talk matter more than programmes, and when a family chooses elective home education in his schools someone now phones to understand rather than to persuade them back.
points: Schools are good at asking families to come and rarely ask why some do not, so listening should come before outreach.
The DfE study's patterns are correlational; helping at school or joining the PTA goes with better outcomes, but that does not mean more parental presence is the cure.
Differences between parental hopes and expectations are socially patterned, so staff from varied backgrounds help schools understand families unlike themselves.
A practical step: when a family chooses home education, call them to understand their reasons, not to talk them out of it.
quotes: During my final years as headteacher at Carclaze, we paid more and more attention to the empty spaces on the parents’ evening booking sheets. Teachers gave up their time to phone the families who hadn’t made appointments. Still, we never reached 100%.
The authors are careful to say that their findings show association, not cause. The data can show what tends to go together, not what makes the difference. But some of the patterns are striking.

Parents who help out at school, join the PTA or sit on governing bodies tend to have children who do better. It would be easy to conclude that we just need more parents in school. The authors warn against exactly that.
The authors point out that the gap between what parents hope for and what they actually expect is itself “socially patterned”. This is where Yates matters most.

During a recent staff listening activity at a CELT secondary school, a member of staff shared their journey from pupil, through an apprenticeship and further training, to leading a department in the same school. I was blown away by the way they could show the difference they make to that school. Their route looked nothing like mine, and the school is far better for it.
None of these is a programme. They are books, libraries and talk.

One line in the limitations section stopped me. Families experiencing the most disadvantage are the most likely to drop out of studies like this over time, so the samples “may underrepresent some of the groups most at risk of poor educational outcomes”.

So, here’s one small step we’ve taken. In our secondary schools, starting with one, when a family chooses elective home education, someone now picks up the phone. Not to persuade them to come back, but to understand.
